questions.title: What Poiseuille's equation determines
questions.question: Which of the following is correct about Poiseuille's equation?

options.A: It determines the factors affecting resistance of blood vessels.
options.B: Resistance is directly proportional to the radius of blood vessels.
options.C: Resistance is inversely proportional to the length of the blood vessel.
options.E: It determines the factors affecting intraluminal pressure of blood vessels.

explanations.A: Correct. Poiseuille's equation is the physical relationship that determines the factors affecting the resistance a blood vessel offers to flow. It states that resistance varies directly with blood viscosity and vessel length, and inversely with the vessel radius raised to the fourth power. This is why radius, the one of the three determinants that changes physiologically, dominates changes in resistance.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Resistance is inversely, not directly, proportional to vessel radius — and specifically to the fourth power of radius, making the relationship far steeper than a simple inverse.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Resistance is directly, not inversely, proportional to vessel length — a longer vessel offers more resistance, not less.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Blood viscosity is one of the three determinants in Poiseuille's equation and does affect resistance, varying directly with it.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Poiseuille's equation determines the factors affecting vascular resistance and flow, not the factors affecting a vessel's own intraluminal pressure.

questions.learning_objective: State that Poiseuille's equation determines the factors (viscosity, length, radius) affecting vascular resistance.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.28

questions.title: A characteristic of turbulent blood flow
questions.question: Turbulent blood flow is characterized by which one of the following?

options.E: Blood flow is below critical velocity.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Streamline (laminar) flow is the opposite pattern from turbulent flow, not a feature of it.
explanations.B: Correct. Turbulent flow is disorganised flow in which eddy currents — swirling, cross-current movements of blood — replace the smooth, layered pattern of laminar flow. It arises once the Reynolds number rises high enough (chiefly through rising velocity or vessel diameter, or falling viscosity), and it is the eddy currents themselves that generate the vibrations detected clinically as murmurs and bruits. Streamline flow, silence, a low Reynolds number and a sub-critical velocity all instead describe laminar, not turbulent, flow.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Turbulent flow generates audible vibrations (murmurs and bruits); it is laminar flow that is silent.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A Reynolds number below roughly 2000 predicts laminar, not turbulent, flow — turbulence requires a HIGH Reynolds number.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Turbulence occurs ABOVE, not below, a vessel's critical velocity.

questions.learning_objective: Identify eddy currents as the defining feature of turbulent blood flow.

questions.title: The exception among peripheral-resistance facts
questions.question: As regards peripheral resistance, all the following are true except:

options.A: The main determinant factor is the change in diameter of arterioles.
options.B: Viscosity of blood is inversely related to peripheral resistance.
options.C: It decreases in anemia and hypoproteinemia.
options.D: Increase in length of vessels, as in the systemic circulation, increases peripheral resistance.

explanations.A: Incorrect (this statement is true). Arteriolar diameter is indeed the main determinant of peripheral resistance, since it is the one Poiseuille variable the body actively and rapidly controls.
explanations.B: Correct — this is the false statement (the exception). Blood viscosity is DIRECTLY, not inversely, related to peripheral resistance: a rise in viscosity raises resistance, and a fall in viscosity (as in anemia or hypoproteinemia) lowers it, exactly the opposite of an inverse relationship. This direct relationship is one of the three determinants named by Poiseuille's law, alongside vessel radius and length.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this statement is true). Anemia and hypoproteinemia both lower blood viscosity, and since viscosity is directly related to resistance, peripheral resistance falls in both conditions.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this statement is true). Vessel length is directly related to resistance by Poiseuille's law, so the longer total vessel length of the systemic circulation (compared with the pulmonary circulation) contributes to its higher resistance.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that blood viscosity is directly, not inversely, related to peripheral resistance.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.28

questions.title: Reynold's number threshold for turbulence
questions.question: Turbulence becomes evident if Reynold's number exceeds:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 200 is far below the range at which turbulence becomes evident.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 100 is far below the range at which turbulence becomes evident.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A Reynolds number of 2000 marks the upper edge of reliably laminar flow, not the point at which turbulence becomes evident — flow between roughly 2000 and 3000 is only transitional.
explanations.D: Correct. Flow is reliably laminar below a Reynolds number of roughly 2000 and becomes reliably turbulent once it exceeds roughly 3000, with the range in between transitional. Above 3000, the eddy currents of turbulent flow are consistently present rather than intermittent. This threshold is why a sufficiently high velocity, wide diameter or low viscosity — all of which raise the Reynolds number — reliably provokes turbulence.

questions.learning_objective: State that turbulence becomes reliably evident once the Reynolds number exceeds roughly 3000.

questions.title: How turbulent flow is detected
questions.question: Turbulent blood flow is detected by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Laplace's law relates wall tension to pressure and radius; it does not predict whether flow is laminar or turbulent.
explanations.B: Correct. The Reynolds number is the dimensionless index used to detect and predict whether blood flow will be laminar or turbulent, rising with velocity, vessel diameter and blood density and falling with viscosity. A high Reynolds number (above roughly 3000) reliably predicts turbulence, while a low one (below roughly 2000) predicts laminar flow. None of the circulation's other named physical laws serves this specific predictive role.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ohm's law (in its hemodynamic analogy, flow = pressure/resistance) describes the magnitude of flow, not whether that flow is laminar or turbulent.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Poiseuille's law describes the factors determining resistance and flow (viscosity, length, radius), not the laminar-versus-turbulent distinction.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the Reynolds number as the index used to detect turbulent blood flow.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.29

questions.title: The resistance vessels of the circulation
questions.question: Resistant vessels are:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Arteries mainly conduct blood under high pressure and contribute comparatively little variable resistance compared with arterioles.
explanations.B: Correct. Arterioles are the principal resistance vessels of the systemic circulation. Their small lumen combined with a well-developed smooth-muscle media lets them change vascular resistance far more than any other vessel type, and by Poiseuille's fourth-power radius relationship, small changes in arteriolar diameter produce large changes in resistance and flow. This makes arterioles, not arteries, capillaries or veins, the site of active resistance control.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Capillaries are the site of exchange, with walls too thin and non-muscular to actively regulate resistance.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Veins are thin-walled, highly compliant capacitance vessels that store blood volume; they are not the circulation's chief resistance vessels.

questions.learning_objective: Identify arterioles as the principal resistance vessels of the systemic circulation.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.29

questions.title: The physiologically variable resistance parameter
questions.question: Choose the variable parameter which affects resistance:

explanations.A: Correct. Of the three Poiseuille determinants of resistance, only vessel radius changes significantly and rapidly under physiological control — vessel length is essentially fixed, and viscosity changes only slowly with haematocrit. This is why radius, acting through arteriolar diameter, is the parameter the body actually varies to regulate resistance moment to moment.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Vessel length is essentially fixed for a given vascular bed and is not a parameter the body varies to regulate resistance.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Viscosity affects resistance but changes only slowly, with haematocrit and plasma protein, not as a moment-to-moment regulatory variable.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Only radius, not length or viscosity, is the physiologically variable determinant this question asks for.

questions.learning_objective: Identify vessel radius as the physiologically variable determinant of resistance.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.29

questions.title: Blood flow and arteriolar dilatation
questions.question: Concerning blood flow (F):

options.C: It increases when the resistance increases.
options.D: It increases due to arteriolar dilatation.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The flow equation is F = ΔP / R (resistance), not radius directly.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Flow increases, not decreases, when the driving pressure gradient (ΔP) increases.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Flow decreases, not increases, when resistance increases — flow and resistance move in opposite directions in F = ΔP / R.
explanations.D: Correct. Blood flow equals the pressure gradient divided by resistance (F = ΔP / R). Arteriolar dilatation sharply lowers resistance, since resistance falls with the fourth power of radius by Poiseuille's law, and a fall in R with ΔP unchanged raises F. This is the mechanism by which arteriolar dilatation increases local and downstream blood flow.

questions.learning_objective: State that blood flow increases with arteriolar dilatation via the F = ΔP/R relationship.

questions.title: Velocity of blood flow at the vessel wall
questions.question: The velocity of blood flow:

options.A: Is higher in the capillaries than in the arterioles.
options.B: Is higher in the veins than in the arteries.
options.C: Is reduced in a constricted area of a blood vessel.
options.D: Falls to almost zero in the layer in contact with the wall of the vessel.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Velocity is LOWER, not higher, in capillaries than in arterioles, because the capillary bed's combined cross-sectional area is far larger.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Velocity is lower in veins than in arteries at a comparable point in the circulation, not higher, since venous total cross-sectional area is larger.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Velocity RISES, not falls, in a constricted (narrowed) segment, since the same volume of blood is forced through a smaller cross-sectional area.
explanations.D: Correct. Laminar flow within a vessel forms a parabolic velocity profile: friction with the vessel wall makes the layer of blood in contact with it essentially stationary, with velocity falling to almost zero there, while velocity is greatest at the vessel's axial centre. This profile underlies why the layer nearest the wall is the slowest-moving part of the flow.

questions.learning_objective: State that blood flow velocity falls to near zero at the vessel wall in laminar flow.

questions.title: The incorrect statement about turbulent flow
questions.question: Which of the following is incorrect concerning turbulent blood flow?

options.A: Turbulent flow is heard only in blood vessels.
options.B: If Reynold's number was more than 3000, turbulent flow will always occur.
options.C: Above a critical velocity, blood flow becomes turbulent.
options.D: Turbulence can create vibrations that can be detected as murmurs.

explanations.A: Correct — this is the incorrect statement. Turbulent-flow murmurs and bruits are audible over the chest and other body surfaces as sound conducted from the turbulent vessel, so the sound is not confined to ("heard only in") the blood vessel itself. The statement overstates where the turbulence is heard, and the other three options here all correctly describe turbulent flow.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this statement is true). Above a Reynolds number of roughly 3000, turbulent flow reliably always occurs, which is the basis of the 3000 threshold this lecture teaches.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this statement is true). Above a vessel's critical velocity — the velocity at which the Reynolds number crosses its upper threshold — flow reliably becomes turbulent.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this statement is true). The eddy currents of turbulent flow generate vibrations that are detected clinically as murmurs and bruits.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the false statement among the standard facts about turbulent blood flow.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.30

questions.title: Greatest influence on blood flow velocity
questions.question: Which of the following factors has the greatest influence on blood flow velocity?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Blood viscosity is a secondary influence on flow velocity compared with vessel diameter.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Vessel length is essentially fixed and has little influence on flow velocity.
explanations.C: Correct. Vessel diameter has the greatest influence on blood flow velocity, because it sets the cross-sectional area available to flow. Across the circulation, velocity is lowest wherever total cross-sectional area is largest — the capillary bed — and highest where it is smallest, regardless of how narrow any single vessel of that type is. This cross-sectional-area effect dominates over viscosity, length or pressure in determining velocity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Blood pressure influences the driving force for flow but has less direct influence on velocity than vessel diameter, which sets the cross-sectional area flow must pass through.

questions.learning_objective: Identify vessel diameter as the factor with the greatest influence on blood flow velocity.

questions.title: Blood flow and vessel diameter
questions.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding blood flow and vessel diameter?

options.A: Blood flow is inversely proportional to vessel diameter.
options.B: Blood flow is directly proportional to vessel diameter.
options.C: Blood flow is not affected by vessel diameter.
options.D: Blood flow is only affected by vessel diameter in arteries.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Blood flow is directly, not inversely, proportional to vessel diameter — a wider vessel carries more flow, not less.
explanations.B: Correct. Following the F = ΔP / R relationship and Poiseuille's fourth-power radius dependence of resistance, blood flow rises steeply as vessel diameter rises, since a wider vessel offers far less resistance. Blood flow is therefore directly proportional to vessel diameter. This holds across vessel types, not only in arteries.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Vessel diameter is one of the most powerful determinants of blood flow, through its effect on resistance.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The diameter-flow relationship applies across vessel types, not only in arteries.

questions.learning_objective: State that blood flow is directly proportional to vessel diameter.

questions.hold: held, physically incorrect key — "How does resistance to blood flow change if the vessel diameter is halved, according to Poiseuille's equation? a) Resistance is halved b) Resistance doubles c) Resistance is quadrupled d) Resistance remains constant" marks (c) "quadrupled" (4x) as correct, but Poiseuille's fourth-power radius law (R ∝ 1/r^4) means halving the radius increases resistance 16-fold, not 4-fold — none of the four printed options states the physically correct answer. Held rather than authored to avoid minting a concept or question that teaches a false relationship.

questions.title: A cause of increased blood viscosity
questions.question: Which of the following conditions could increase blood viscosity?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Anemia lowers, rather than raises, blood viscosity, since it reduces the concentration of red blood cells.
explanations.B: Correct. Dehydration reduces the plasma (fluid) volume relative to the cellular volume of blood, effectively haemoconcentrating it. Because blood viscosity is set chiefly by haematocrit (red-cell concentration), this haemoconcentration raises viscosity. Anemia and hypoproteinemia instead lower the concentration of red cells or plasma protein and so lower viscosity, the opposite effect.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Low cholesterol is not a determinant of blood viscosity, which is set chiefly by haematocrit and plasma protein.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vasodilation changes a vessel's diameter and resistance; it does not raise the viscosity of the blood itself.

questions.learning_objective: Identify dehydration as a cause of increased blood viscosity, via haemoconcentration.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.30

questions.title: Effect of increased resistance-vessel radius
questions.question: When the radius of the resistance vessels is increased, which of the following is increased?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Increasing resistance-vessel (arteriolar) radius lowers, rather than raises, resistance and so tends to lower rather than raise systolic pressure.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Increasing arteriolar radius lowers total peripheral resistance, and diastolic pressure — which depends heavily on peripheral resistance — falls rather than rises.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Blood viscosity is unaffected by arteriolar radius; it is set by haematocrit and plasma protein, not vessel diameter.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Haematocrit is a property of the blood itself and is not changed by a change in resistance-vessel radius.
explanations.E: Correct. When the radius of the resistance vessels (arterioles) increases, resistance falls sharply by Poiseuille's fourth-power relationship, and by F = ΔP / R, flow through that bed and into the downstream capillaries rises. Capillary blood flow is therefore what increases when resistance-vessel radius increases, not blood pressure, viscosity or haematocrit.

questions.learning_objective: State that increasing resistance-vessel radius raises downstream capillary blood flow.
